939.title: Gujrat and annexation, 1849
939.hook: the last battle is lost, the soldiers lay down their arms, and the Punjab is annexed
939.howItsDone: Sikh histories mark the defeat at Gujrat and the annexation that followed as the end of the Sikh kingdom of the Punjab, and the story of the soldiers laying down their arms is still told at gatherings about that history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chillianwala, and your line was they held. Where did you stay put for one breath longer? Today, the holding ends. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

A line of soldiers comes forward, one by one, and lays down its weapons on a pile. Swords, matchlocks, shields. These are men of the Khalsa army, and the war is over. There's a story told about that day. An old soldier, setting down his arms, says quietly that today Ranjit Singh has died. The Maharaja was long dead. But the kingdom he built was ending in front of them. Today: Gujrat and annexation.
screen: `WEAPONS LAID ON A PILE.` → `TODAY RANJIT SINGH HAS DIED.` → `A KINGDOM ENDING.`

segments.voice: First, the battle. Gujrat here is a town in the Punjab, not the Indian state of a similar name. After Chillianwala, the British waited for more troops, and above all more heavy guns. At Gujrat they used them. A long, heavy bombardment came before the infantry moved, and this time the Sikh line broke. Second, the surrender. The British pursued the retreating army. Its leaders, Sher Singh Attariwala and his father Chattar Singh, gave themselves up, and the soldiers handed over their arms. That's where the story of the old soldier is set. It may be remembered more than recorded, but Sikhs have kept telling it because it says what the day meant. Third, the annexation. Lord Dalhousie did not restore the court at Lahore. He declared the Punjab part of British India. The boy Maharaja, Duleep Singh, still a child, was made to put his name to terms that gave up his kingdom and his claims to it. The flag over the fort at Lahore was changed. Fourth, what Sikh scripture says about endings. In his saloks near the close of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes a person whose strength has gone, who is bound and can find no way out. And in the next breath the verse turns: strength returns, the bonds fall away, and everything is in the Lord's hands. The Guru doesn't pretend the binding isn't real. He just doesn't stop the verse there. A kingdom did end at Gujrat, and the story of the old soldier doesn't hide it. That's today's line.

940.title: The diamond sent away
940.hook: the Koh-i-Noor is taken from the boy king and sent to Queen Victoria
940.howItsDone: The Koh-i-Noor remains in the British crown jewels, and in Sikh tellings of the annexation it stands for everything taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh as a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujrat and annexation, and your line was the kingdom ended. What ending did you sit with? Today, a stone that stood for that kingdom leaves it. Day nine hundred forty.

A small box, and inside it a single great diamond. Ranjit Singh wore it on his arm at court. Before him, Afghan rulers had held it, and Mughal emperors before them. Its name, the Koh-i-Noor, is usually given in English as the mountain of light. When the Punjab was annexed, the terms said this stone would go to the Queen of England. And it was taken from a boy who was still a child. Today: the diamond sent away.
screen: `A STONE IN A SMALL BOX.` → `WORN ON A MAHARAJA'S ARM.` → `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the stone. The Koh-i-Noor had passed from ruler to ruler, often by force. Ranjit Singh obtained it from an Afghan king, Shah Shuja, who had come to him as a refugee, and the circumstances are still argued over. At Lahore it became a sign of the kingdom itself. Second, the terms. When Lord Dalhousie annexed the Punjab, the agreement named the Koh-i-Noor and said it was to be surrendered to the Queen. Dalhousie wanted it sent as a prize of the war, not as a gift from the Maharaja. Third, the journey. A story is told in the life of John Lawrence, one of the officers then governing the Punjab, that the stone was handed to him in its little box and he slipped it into a pocket and forgot it, until he was asked for it and had a bad moment searching. Then it was carried under guard to the coast and shipped to Britain. Fourth, what remains. In Britain the stone was cut down to a new shape, and it became part of the crown jewels. Its return has been asked for, from more than one country, and the question is still open. In Sikh tellings of this history, the diamond isn't really about wealth. It's about a child who lost his kingdom and then lost the sign of it too. Guru Nanak, in a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib that tradition links to the invasion of Babur, says that for the sake of wealth, many were ruined and disgraced; it can't be gathered without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go with you when you die. That's today's line.

941.title: The boy far from home
941.hook: Duleep Singh, still a child, is raised by British guardians and baptized a Christian
941.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell Duleep Singh's childhood under British guardianship as part of the loss of the kingdom, and his baptism is read differently in different accounts: as his own choice, or as the result of being separated from his mother and his faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the diamond sent away, and your line was taken away. What did you let go of, even for a minute? Today, the boy the diamond was taken from. Day nine hundred forty-one.

A garden by the Ganges at Fatehgarh, a long way from Lahore. A boy with a pony, a tutor, a few servants, and a Scottish doctor who has been put in charge of him. The boy has been a Maharaja. He has sat on his father's throne, been bowed to by generals, worn the jewels of the Punjab. Now he has lessons, a garden and guardians. His mother has been sent away, and the court he knew is gone. Today: the boy far from home.
screen: `A GARDEN AT FATEHGARH.` → `A BOY WHO WAS A MAHARAJA.` → `LESSONS, AND GUARDIANS.`

segments.voice: First, the guardian. After the annexation, Duleep Singh was placed in the care of Dr. John Login, who had looked after the treasury at Lahore. Login and his wife, Lena, raised him. Her later book about the boy is warm toward him, and also plainly written from the guardians' side. Second, the move. The boy was taken out of the Punjab to Fatehgarh, away from the Sikh court, the gurdwaras of Lahore and anyone who might raise him as a Sikh king. The British saw a boy who could become a rallying point. So they kept him far away. Third, the baptism. In those years, while still a boy in his early teens, Duleep Singh asked to become a Christian, and he was baptized. The Login account says the wish was his own, that he'd been listening to a household servant read from the Bible. Some Sikh writers see it differently: a child cut off from his mother, his faith and his people, who was shaped by the only adults left around him. Both readings are still held, and the sources can't fully settle what was in a child's heart. Fourth, what Sikh scripture offers a lonely child. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Bilaval, in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says the hot wind does not touch the one who shelters in the Lord: a protecting line is drawn on every side, and no pain comes near. Those words were there, in the scripture of the faith he was raised away from. That's today's line.

942.title: An English country house
942.hook: Duleep lives as a gentleman in Suffolk, far from the Punjab
942.howItsDone: Elveden Hall in Suffolk is remembered in Sikh history as Duleep Singh's English home, and Sikh visitors to Britain sometimes travel there to see the place where Maharaja Duleep Singh lived.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy far from home, and your line was a boy far away. Which child came to mind? Today, the boy is grown, and further away than ever. Day nine hundred forty-two.

Shotguns crack across a cold, sandy heath in Suffolk. Beaters walk the fields, birds go up, and the gentlemen fire. The host of the shooting party is known as a remarkable shot. He owns the house, the woods and the land around it. He dines with the Prince of Wales. He has been received by Queen Victoria. And he was born a Maharaja of the Punjab. Today: an English country house.
screen: `SHOTGUNS OVER A SUFFOLK HEATH.` → `THE HOST IS A FINE SHOT.` → `BORN A MAHARAJA.`

segments.voice: First, the move to England. In his teens, Duleep Singh was brought to Britain. The Queen took an interest in him, and he was welcomed at court as an exotic and charming guest. He was paid an allowance by the government that had taken his kingdom, and it was never as much as he thought was owed. Second, the house. He bought an estate called Elveden, in Suffolk, and rebuilt the hall. Inside, some of the rooms were made to look like an Indian palace, with carved arches and rich ornament, set in the middle of the English countryside. Outside, he turned the land into a great shooting estate. Third, the life. He married, and his wife, Bamba Müller, had grown up in Cairo. Their children were raised as English gentry. He shot, entertained, spent heavily and fell into debt. From the outside, the picture was complete: an English gentleman with an Indian title. Fourth, what was underneath. The rooms that looked like a palace tell their own story. A man who had everything a country house can offer still built a piece of the home he had lost into its walls. In a hymn of Guru Arjan in the Guru Granth Sahib, which tradition says was written in longing for the Guru's presence, he says his mind yearns for the sight of the Guru, crying out like the rainbird crying for rain, and that he can't sleep or rest without it. Some Sikh readers of Duleep's story hear that ache in the Indian rooms at Elveden. That's today's line.

943.title: Mother and son again, 1861
943.hook: after long years apart, Duleep meets his mother, and she tells him of his heritage
943.carry: she told him who he was
943.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Maharani Jind Kaur as a mother who never stopped resisting the loss of her son and her kingdom, and the meeting in Calcutta is told as the moment Duleep Singh began to recover his heritage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an English country house, and your line was far from punjab. Where did your mind go when you asked where you belong? Today, someone arrives who remembers. Day nine hundred forty-three.

What do you say to a mother you last saw when you were small? A hotel in Calcutta. A grown man in English clothes waits in a room. The door opens, and a woman comes in, older than he remembers, her eyesight failing. She is Maharani Jind Kaur, the queen who was sent away. When she reaches him, the story goes, she runs her hands over his head, looking for his uncut hair, and finds it cut short. Today: mother and son again.
screen: `A HOTEL IN CALCUTTA.` → `A QUEEN WHOSE EYES ARE FAILING.` → `HER HANDS ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: First, where she had been. After she was separated from her son and sent away, Jind Kaur was held as a prisoner. She escaped, in disguise, and made her way to Nepal, where she lived in exile under the protection of its rulers. All those years, letters between mother and son were watched or stopped. Second, the meeting. Duleep Singh asked to see her, and in time the British allowed it, as long as she did not go back to the Punjab. They met in Calcutta. The boy she had last held was now a grown man, a Christian, living as an English gentleman. Third, what she told him. Jind Kaur came with him to England and lived near him in London. She talked to him about the Punjab, about his father, Ranjit Singh, about the kingdom and how it was lost, and about the Sikh faith he had been raised away from. Histories that follow his life mark this as the moment something in him began to turn. Fourth, a mother's blessing in the Guru Granth Sahib. There's a hymn of Guru Arjan in which a mother speaks to her son: this is your mother's blessing, son, that you never forget the Lord for even an instant. The blessing is about remembering the Lord. In Calcutta, and then in London, this mother's gift was a remembering too: she gave her son back the story of who he was. That's today's line.

944.title: Jind Kaur's death, 1863
944.hook: she dies in London, and her son takes her ashes toward India
944.howItsDone: At a Sikh funeral, hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are placed in flowing water; Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories and gatherings about the end of the kingdom.

In a rented house in Kensington, with London's carriages passing in the street, a queen of the Punjab is dying. She has been a regent, a prisoner, a fugitive across the hills to Nepal, and, at the end, a mother living near her son. She will not see Lahore again. And when she dies, her son faces a question no English gentleman is trained for: how do you take your mother home? Today: Jind Kaur's death.
screen: `A RENTED HOUSE IN KENSINGTON.` → `A QUEEN WHO WON'T SEE LAHORE.` → `HOW DO YOU TAKE HER HOME?`

segments.voice: First, her last years. Jind Kaur lived in London near Duleep Singh after their meeting in Calcutta. Her health was poor and her sight was failing. But she kept telling him about the Punjab, and the histories suggest the stories took hold. Second, her death. She died in London, far from the land she had ruled as regent. Sikh custom is to cremate the body. In Victorian London that was not a simple thing to arrange, and her son wanted her rites done in India, not in England. Third, the journey. Duleep Singh took his mother's body by sea toward India. But he was not permitted to take her into the Punjab. So she was cremated on the banks of the Godavari river at Nasik, far to the south of the land she had known. A small memorial was built there. Her ashes, tradition says, were later moved to Lahore and laid near her husband's memorial, though that came long afterward. Fourth, how Sikh scripture speaks of death. In the Alahniyan, the songs of mourning by Guru Nanak in the Guru Granth Sahib, he says that whoever has come must rise and go, and that this world is a passing show. At a Sikh funeral the hymns are sung, the body is cremated, and the ashes are given to flowing water. A son who had been raised far from all of it did what he could to carry his mother home, and got as close as he was allowed. That's today's line.

945.hook: stopped at Aden on his way to India, he takes amrit again
945.howItsDone: Sikhs take amrit, the Khalsa initiation, in a ceremony led by initiated Sikhs, and Duleep Singh's initiation at Aden is remembered as his return to the faith of his parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jind Kaur's death, and your line was ashes carried home. Whose name did you say aloud? Today, her son tries to go home himself. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Officials climb aboard a steamer that has just tied up at a hot, rocky port, where ships bound for India stop to take on coal. They have orders for one of the passengers: he may go no further. The port is Aden. The passenger, traveling east with his family, is Duleep Singh. He has left England and set out for India, and he has told the Sikhs he is coming. He will never reach them. But in this port, something happens anyway. Today: Duleep returns to Sikhi.
screen: `A COALING PORT CALLED ADEN.` → `ORDERS: NO FURTHER.` → `SOMETHING HAPPENS ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. After his mother's stories, Duleep Singh began to read about the Sikh faith and about the annexation. He came to believe the terms that took his kingdom were unjust, and that the British owed him more than his allowance. He grew bitter, and he decided to go back to India and to the faith of his father. Second, the voyage. He set out by sea, and he wrote openly to the Sikhs that he was returning to them. The British government did not want him in India, where he might become a rallying point. So he was stopped at Aden. Third, the amrit. There, in a foreign port, Duleep Singh took amrit, the Khalsa initiation, from Sikhs who had come for it. The man who had been baptized a Christian as a boy was initiated as a Sikh as a grown man. He never reached the Punjab. But he had come back. Fourth, a song of joy addressed to a mother. In the Anand Sahib, Guru Amar Das opens with a cry of joy addressed to his mother: joy has come, mother, for I have found the true Guru. A mother who told her son who he was, and a son who came back to it, in the place where he was told he could go no further. And a look back at the week. Gujrat and annexation, the diamond sent away, the boy at Fatehgarh, the house in Suffolk, a mother found again and then lost. All week the story has moved away from the Punjab. Today, in the port where he was stopped, it turns toward it. That's today's line.
screen: `THE TURN TOWARD HOME.` · `STOPPED AT ADEN.` · `AMRIT IN A FOREIGN PORT.` · `JOY HAS COME, MOTHER.` · then, large: `HE CAME BACK.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something you left. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you once loved and let go of: a practice, a language, a friend, a place, a habit of kindness. Don't judge yourself for leaving it. Just picture what coming back to it would look like, in the smallest possible way. One page. One phone call. One quiet minute. Breathe with that picture. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Duleep returns to Sikhi. Stopped at Aden on his way to India, Duleep Singh took amrit and came back to the faith of his father and mother. Today's word.
Your line: he came back. Today, take one small step back toward something you left, even if you can't go all the way. Day nine hundred forty-five.

fork.setup: you're Duleep Singh. officials at Aden tell you you may go no further toward India. what do you do there, as the histories tell it?
options: give up and sail back to England quietly.
take amrit there, in the port.
slip away to India in disguise.
fork.reveal: he took amrit at Aden; he never reached the Punjab, but he had come back to Sikhi.

original.note: amrit, the nectar of the Khalsa initiation; taking amrit is how a Sikh joins the Khalsa.

trapdoor: what you thought: Duleep Singh went home to the Punjab.
what it means: he set out for India, was stopped at Aden, and took amrit there.
what a scholar hears: the British stopped him because they feared he would become a rallying point, and his return to Sikhi was bound up with his claims about the annexation.
